claim: Cytoplasmic dynein-1 (dynein) is a 1.4 MDa, multi-subunit motor complex responsible for the vast majority of cargo transport towards the minus ends of microtubules in eukaryotic cells.
source: Cytoplasmic dynein-1 (hereafter referred to as dynein) is a 1.4 MDa, multi-subunit motor complex that is responsible for the vast majority of cargo transport towards the minus ends of microtubules in eukaryotic cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous literature (Carter et al., 2016; Dodding and Way, 2011; Hoogenraad and Akhmanova, 2016) establishing dynein's role in cargo transport.

claim: Dynein's cargoes include organelles, vesicles, aggregated proteins, mRNAs and pathogenic viruses.
source: Dynein's cargoes include organelles, vesicles, aggregated proteins, mRNAs and pathogenic viruses (Carter et al., 2016; Dodding and Way, 2011; Hoogenraad and Akhmanova, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies documenting the various types of cargoes transported by dynein.

claim: Dynein plays important roles in organising microtubules in mitotic and interphase cells.
source: In addition to its function on motile cargoes, dynein plays important roles in organising microtubules in mitotic and interphase cells (e.g. Bader and Vaughan, 2010; Dujardin et al., 2003; Dujardin and Vallee, 2002; Koonce et al., 1999; Laan et al., 2012; Nguyen-Ngoc et al., 2007; Ten Hoopen et al., 2012; Varma et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to previous research demonstrating dynein's role in microtubule organization.

claim: Microtubule plus ends alternate between phases of polymerisation ('growth') and depolymerisation ('shrinkage')—a process known as dynamic instability.
source: Whereas the microtubule minus ends are often stabilised in vivo, the plus ends alternate between phases of polymerisation ('growth') and depolymerisation ('shrinkage')—a process known as dynamic instability.
evidence: This claim represents established knowledge about microtubule dynamics.

claim: Microtubule plus ends are stabilised during growth by a cap of tubulin-GTP, with depolymerisation triggered when the GTP bound to β-tubulin at the microtubule tip is hydrolysed.
source: Microtubule plus ends are stabilised during growth by a cap of tubulin-GTP, with depolymerisation triggered when the GTP bound to β-tubulin at the microtubule tip is hydrolysed (Carlier, 1982; Mitchison and Kirschner, 1984).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to foundational studies on microtubule dynamics.

claim: Dynein is detected along the lattice of the microtubule, but is enriched at the plus end in a wide variety of eukaryotic cells.
source: Dynein is detected along the lattice of the microtubule, but is enriched at the plus end in a wide variety of eukaryotic cells (Han et al., 2001; Kobayashi and Murayama, 2009; Lee et al., 2003; Lenz et al., 2006; Ma and Chisholm, 2002; Moughamian et al., 2013; Schuster et al., 2011; Sheeman et al., 2003; Splinter et al., 2012; Vaughan et al., 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations documenting dynein localization at microtubule plus ends.

claim: Association of dynein with the plus end is important for efficient initiation of retrograde cargo transport in polarised cells, including neurons.
source: Association of the motor complex with the plus end is important for its microtubule organising functions at the cell cortex (Lee et al., 2003; Markus and Lee, 2011a, 2011b; Sheeman et al., 2003) and for efficient initiation of retrograde cargo transport in polarised cells, including neurons (Lenz et al., 2006; Lloyd et al., 2012; Moughamian and Holzbaur, 2012; Moughamian et al., 2013; Zhang et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies showing the role of plus-end localization in cargo transport initiation.

claim: p150 is a subunit of the dynactin complex.
source: A key player in this process is p150Glued (hereafter p150), a subunit of the dynactin complex.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the composition of the dynactin complex.

claim: Dynactin is a 1.1 MDa complex of 11 distinct components that co-precipitates with dynein.
source: Dynactin is a 1.1 MDa complex of 11 distinct components that co-precipitates with dynein and is critical for its plus-end targeting and cargo transport functions in vivo (Moughamian et al., 2013; Schroer, 2004; Splinter et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations describing the properties of the dynactin complex.

claim: Dynactin is critical for dynein's plus-end targeting and cargo transport functions in vivo.
source: Dynactin is a 1.1 MDa complex of 11 distinct components that co-precipitates with dynein and is critical for its plus-end targeting and cargo transport functions in vivo (Moughamian et al., 2013; Schroer, 2004; Splinter et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies demonstrating dynactin's functional importance.

claim: p150 contains a CAP-Gly domain that can bind directly to members of the end-binding (EB) protein family such as EB1 or EB3.
source: p150 contains a CAP-Gly domain that can bind directly to members of the end-binding (EB) protein family such as EB1 or EB3 (Bjelić et al., 2012; Honnappa et al., 2006).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to structural and biochemical studies.

claim: EB proteins dynamically track polymerising plus ends through repeated transient binding events on a structure associated with the GTP- or GDP.Pi-tubulin conformation.
source: EB proteins dynamically track polymerising plus ends through repeated transient binding events on a structure associated with the GTP- or GDP.Pi-tubulin conformation (Akhmanova and Steinmetz, 2015; Bieling et al., 2008, 2007; Maurer et al., 2011, 2012; Zanic et al., 2009; Zhang et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations documenting EB protein behavior.

claim: p150 can contact the intermediate chain of the dynein complex.
source: p150 can also contact the intermediate chain of the dynein complex (Karki and Holzbaur, 1995; King et al., 2003; Vaughan and Vallee, 1995).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to biochemical studies.

claim: A truncated version of a tissue-specific p150 isoform induces tracking of the human dynein complex on EB1-associated plus ends of growing microtubules in vitro.
source: Consistent with this model, a truncated version of a tissue-specific p150 isoform induces tracking of the human dynein complex on EB1-associated plus ends of growing microtubules in vitro (Duellberg et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a previous in vitro reconstitution study.

claim: Individual mammalian dynein complexes rarely exhibit processive motion.
source: Reconstituting this process in vitro has been very challenging because individual mammalian dynein complexes rarely exhibit processive motion (McKenney et al., 2014; Miura et al., 2010; Schlager et al., 2014; Trokter et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple in vitro studies.

claim: Association of dynein with both the dynactin complex and a cargo adaptor results in frequent processive movements along microtubules.
source: Association of dynein with both the dynactin complex and a cargo adaptor results in frequent processive movements along microtubules.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to recent studies (McKenney et al., 2014; Olenick et al., 2016; Schlager et al., 2014; Schroeder and Vale, 2016).

claim: In the context of a dynein-dynactin-cargo adaptor complex, the motor translocates faster and has a greater force output.
source: In the context of a dynein-dynactin-cargo adaptor complex, the motor also translocates faster and has a greater force output (Belyy et al., 2016; McKenney et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to studies characterizing dynein-dynactin-cargo adaptor complexes.

claim: BICD2 is a coiled-coil protein that links dynein to several cargoes, including Golgi-derived vesicles and nuclear pore complexes.
source: The activating cargo adaptor that is best characterised is Bicaudal-D2 (BICD2), a coiled-coil protein that links dynein to several cargoes, including Golgi-derived vesicles and nuclear pore complexes (Hoogenraad and Akhmanova, 2016; Hoogenraad et al., 2003; Splinter et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations documenting BICD2's role as a cargo adaptor.

claim: BICD2 uses its N-terminal regions (BICD2N) to associate with dynein and dynactin and its C-terminal regions to recruit cargoes.
source: BICD2 uses its N-terminal regions (BICD2N) to associate with dynein and dynactin and its C-terminal regions to recruit cargoes (Hoogenraad and Akhmanova, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a review summarizing BICD2 structure-function relationships.

claim: Reduced expression of LIS1 causes the neurodevelopmental disease type 1 lissencephaly in humans by perturbing neuronal proliferation and migration.
source: Reduced expression of LIS1 causes the neurodevelopmental disease type 1 lissencephaly in humans by perturbing neuronal proliferation and migration (Moon and Wynshaw-Boris, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a review on lissencephaly.

claim: LIS1 is essential for enrichment of dynein at dynamic microtubule plus ends in mammalian cells.
source: LIS1 forms a homodimer (Kim et al., 2004) that interacts directly with the dynein complex (Huang et al., 2012; McKenney et al., 2010; Sasaki et al., 2000; Tai et al., 2002; Toropova et al., 2014) and is essential for its enrichment at dynamic microtubule plus ends in mammalian cells (Splinter et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a cell biological study.

claim: LIS1 is not needed for association of dynactin with plus ends.
source: LIS1 is not, however, needed for association of dynactin with plus ends (Splinter et al., 2012), suggesting a specific role in recruitment of dynein to these sites.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a cell biological study and represents an inference about LIS1's specific role.

claim: LIS1 is required for efficient transport of many dynein-associated cargoes.
source: In addition to regulating association of dynein with microtubule plus ends, LIS1 is required for efficient transport of many dynein-associated cargoes (Dix et al., 2013; Egan et al., 2012; Lam et al., 2010; Lenz et al., 2006; Pandey and Smith, 2011; Reddy et al., 2016; Splinter et al., 2012; Yi et al, 2011; Zhang et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to studies in various systems.

claim: LIS1 increases the affinity of the isolated motor complex for microtubules.
source: In vitro experiments have shown that LIS1 increases the affinity of the isolated motor complex for microtubules and suppresses its mechanochemical activity (Huang et al., 2012; McKenney et al., 2010; Torisawa et al., 2014; Toropova et al., 2014; Yamada et al., 2013, 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple in vitro studies.

claim: LIS1 suppresses the mechanochemical activity of isolated dynein.
source: In vitro experiments have shown that LIS1 increases the affinity of the isolated motor complex for microtubules and suppresses its mechanochemical activity (Huang et al., 2012; McKenney et al., 2010; Torisawa et al., 2014; Toropova et al., 2014; Yamada et al., 2013, 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple in vitro studies.

claim: LIS1 promotes plus-end tracking of dynein on both growing and shrinking plus ends in the presence of dynactin and EB1.
source: LIS1 promotes dynactin-dependent tracking of dynein on both growing and shrinking plus ends.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript (Figures 2 and 8).

claim: LIS1 increases the frequency and velocity of processive dynein movements that are activated by complex formation with dynactin and a cargo adaptor.
source: LIS1 also increases the frequency and velocity of processive dynein movements that are activated by complex formation with dynactin and a cargo adaptor.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript (Figures 5 and 6).

claim: The stimulatory effect of LIS1 on dynein-dynactin-cargo adaptor complexes contrasts sharply with its documented ability to inhibit the activity of isolated dyneins.
source: This stimulatory effect of LIS1 contrasts sharply with its documented ability to inhibit the activity of isolated dyneins.
evidence: This claim represents an inference based on comparison of the current study's findings with previous literature.

claim: In the presence of both EB1 and the native dynactin complex, a subset of microtubule-associated Alexa647-dynein complexes exhibited binding events that followed the trajectory of the growing plus end for ≥1.8 s.
source: In the presence of both EB1 and the native dynactin complex, which was purified from pig brain, a subset of microtubule-associated Alexa647-dynein complexes exhibited binding events that followed the trajectory of the growing plus end for ≥1.8 s (Figure 2A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A,B.

claim: The mean duration of dynein tracking events at the plus end in the presence of EB1 and dynactin was ~4 s.
source: The mean and maximal duration of dynein tracking events at the plus end in these conditions was ~4 and ~9 s, respectively (Figure 2C,D).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 2C,D.

claim: Tracking behavior of dynein was almost never observed when dynein was mixed with only EB1 or only dynactin.
source: Tracking behaviour was almost never observed when dynein was mixed with only EB1 or only dynactin (Figure 2A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A,B.

claim: EB1 and the full dynactin complex can act together to promote association of dynein with the plus ends of growing microtubules.
source: Thus, EB1 and the full dynactin complex can act together to promote association of dynein with the plus ends of growing microtubules.
evidence: This claim represents a conclusion drawn from the experimental data in Figure 2.

claim: LIS1 strongly increased the number of plus-end tracking events induced by the combination of dynactin and EB1.
source: LIS1 did, however, strongly increase the number of plus-end tracking events induced by the combination of dynactin and EB1 (Figure 2A,B), without changing the duration of microtubule growth phases (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 2A,B and Figure 2—figure supplement 2A.

claim: The duration of dynein tracking events on the growing plus end in the presence of EB1 and dynactin was strongly increased by LIS1.
source: The duration of dynein tracking events on the growing plus end in the presence of EB1 and dynactin was also strongly increased by LIS1 (Figure 2A,C,D); the mean duration of tracking events increased by more than three-fold, with a subset of motor complexes remaining bound to the growing plus ends for longer than 30 s (Figure 2C,D).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 2A,C,D.

claim: LIS1 strongly increases the frequency and duration of tracking events of dynein on the plus end of growing microtubules in conjunction with EB1 and dynactin.
source: We conclude from these experiments that LIS1 strongly increases the frequency and duration of tracking events of dynein on the plus end of growing microtubules in conjunction with EB1 and dynactin.
evidence: This claim represents a conclusion drawn from the experimental data in Figure 2.

claim: The presence of both EB1 and dynactin in the chamber made dynein approximately twice as likely to land at the plus-end site than at the lattice site.
source: The presence of both EB1 and dynactin in the chamber made dynein approximately twice as likely to land at the plus-end site than at the lattice site (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2B.

claim: The addition of LIS1 to EB1 and dynactin did not further increase the frequency of dynein complexes landing on the plus end vs the lattice site.
source: The addition of LIS1 to these proteins did not further increase the frequency of dynein complexes landing on the plus end vs the lattice site (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2B.

claim: LIS1 increases the frequency of tracking events by prolonging the association of dynein with the growing plus end after it has been targeted to this site by EB1 and dynactin.
source: Collectively, these data indicate that LIS1 increases the frequency of tracking events by prolonging the association of dynein with the growing plus end after it has been targeted to this site by EB1 and dynactin.
evidence: This claim represents an inference drawn from the experimental data in Figure 2 and Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: In the presence of EB1 and dynactin, LIS1 increased the duration of plus-end tracking events by dynein but there was no significant change in the duration of lattice binding events.
source: Interestingly, in the same assays in which LIS1 increased the duration of plus-end tracking events by dynein in the presence of EB1 and dynactin, there was no significant change in the duration of lattice binding events (Figure 2E).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: LIS1 specifically increased the persistence of EB1- and dynactin-dependent binding of dynein at the plus end of growing microtubules.
source: Thus, LIS1 specifically increased the persistence of EB1- and dynactin-dependent binding of dynein at the plus end of growing microtubules.
evidence: This claim represents a conclusion drawn from the experimental data in Figure 2E.

claim: TMR-LIS1 was detected with the vast majority of Alexa647-dynein complexes tracking the growing plus end.
source: TMR-LIS1 was detected with the vast majority of Alexa647-dynein complexes tracking the growing plus end (Figure 2F, Figure 2—figure supplement 3A), suggesting that LIS1 directly regulates dynein behaviour at this site.
evidence: This claim is supported by co-localization data shown in Figure 2F and Figure 2—figure supplement 3A.

claim: TMR-LIS1 was detected on a large proportion of dynein complexes that were associated with the lattice.
source: TMR-LIS1 was also detected on a large proportion of dynein complexes that were associated with the lattice (Figure 2F, Figure 2—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by co-localization data shown in Figure 2F and Figure 2—figure supplement 3B.

claim: LIS1 can associate with dynein at the growing plus end and on the lattice, but increases the duration of microtubule binding events only at the former site.
source: We conclude that LIS1 can associate with dynein at the growing plus end and on the lattice, but increases the duration of microtubule binding events only at the former site.
evidence: This claim represents a conclusion drawn from the experimental data in Figure 2.

claim: LIS1 does not influence the dwell time of human dynein on the microtubule lattice.
source: The observation that LIS1 does not influence the dwell time of human dynein on the microtubule lattice was unexpected as yeast LIS1 strongly increases the dwell time of monomeric yeast dynein on stabilised microtubules in the presence of ATP (Huang et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 3 and represents a comparison with previous literature.

claim: Using the same relative concentration of LIS1 to dynein used in dynamic microtubule assays, no influence of LIS1 on the dwell time of the motor complex on the lattice was detected.
source: Using the same relative concentration of LIS1 to dynein used in our dynamic microtubule assays, we again detected no influence of LIS1 on the dwell time of the motor complex on the lattice (Figure 3A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 3A,B.

claim: The rate at which dynein complexes landed on microtubules was not significantly influenced by LIS1 at a 20-fold molar excess.
source: The rate at which dynein complexes landed on microtubules was also not significantly influenced by LIS1 in these experiments (Figure 3A,C).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 3A,C.

claim: A 300-fold molar excess of LIS1 to dynein did not increase the dwell time of the motor complex on microtubules.
source: Even a 300-fold molar excess of LIS1 to dynein did not increase the dwell time of the motor complex on microtubules (Figure 3A,B, Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 3A,B and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: At a 300-fold molar excess of LIS1 to dynein, there was an approximately three-fold increase in dynein's landing rate on the lattice.
source: However, in this condition, there was an approximately three-fold increase in dynein's landing rate on the lattice (Figure 3A,C).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 3A,C.

claim: A high relative concentration of LIS1 to dynein can increase the association of single motor complexes with microtubules by increasing the on-rate.
source: Thus, a high relative concentration of LIS1 to dynein can increase the association of single motor complexes with microtubules by increasing the on-rate.
evidence: This claim represents a conclusion drawn from the experimental data in Figure 3.

claim: Human LIS1 is not sufficient to increase the dwell time of individual human dynein complexes on microtubules.
source: Collectively, our data suggest that, unlike the situation with yeast proteins, human LIS1 is not sufficient to increase the dwell time of individual human dynein complexes on microtubules.
evidence: This claim represents a conclusion drawn from the experimental data in Figure 3 and comparison with yeast studies.

claim: LIS1 can increase the dwell time of human dynein complexes at the plus ends of growing microtubules, which are recruited through EB1 and dynactin.
source: LIS1 can, however, increase the dwell time of human dynein complexes at the plus ends of growing microtubules, which are recruited through EB1 and dynactin.
evidence: This claim represents a conclusion drawn from the experimental data in Figure 2.

claim: In the absence of EB1, minus end-directed movements of dynein-dynactin-BICD2N complexes were just as likely to initiate from the plus end as they were from a randomly selected segment of the GDP lattice of the same length.
source: In the absence of EB1, minus end-directed movements of dynein-dynactin-BICD2N complexes were just as likely to initiate from the plus end as they were from a randomly selected segment of the GDP lattice of the same length (Figure 4A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 4A,B.

claim: Addition of EB1 resulted in minus end-directed transport events being six times more likely to initiate at the plus-end location.
source: Strikingly, addition of EB1 resulted in minus end-directed transport events being six times more likely to initiate at the plus-end location (Figure 4A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 4A,B.

claim: The velocity and run length of processive dynein-dynactin-BICD2N movements in the presence of EB1 did not differ significantly depending on an initiation site on the lattice vs at the plus end.
source: The velocity and run length of processive dynein-dynactin-BICD2N movements in the presence of EB1 did not differ significantly depending on an initiation site on the lattice vs at the plus end (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: EB1 can direct the site of dynein-dynactin-BICD2N transport initiation to the plus end of growing microtubules but this does not influence the motile properties of the complex.
source: Thus, EB1 can direct the site of dynein-dynactin-BICD2N transport initiation to the plus end of growing microtubules but this does not influence the motile properties of the complex.
evidence: This claim represents a conclusion drawn from the experimental data in Figure 4 and Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: In the presence of EB1, dynactin, BICD2N and LIS1, a six-fold higher frequency in the initiation of processive dynein movements from the plus end vs an equivalently-sized GDP lattice site was observed.
source: In the presence of EB1, dynactin, BICD2N and LIS1, we again observed a six-fold higher frequency in the initiation of processive dynein movements from the plus end vs an equivalently-sized GDP lattice site (Figure 4A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 4A,B.

claim: LIS1 did not alter EB1's ability to bias transport initiation to the plus end.
source: Thus, LIS1 did not alter EB1's ability to bias transport initiation to the plus end.
evidence: This claim represents a conclusion drawn from the experimental data in Figure 4A,B.

claim: LIS1 stimulated both the frequency and duration of plus-end tracking events on growing microtubules in the presence of EB1, dynactin and BICD2N.
source: LIS1 did, however, stimulate both the frequency and duration of plus-end tracking events on growing microtubules in the presence of EB1, dynactin and BICD2N, without affecting the duration of static binding events by the motor on the lattice (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C–G).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C–G.

claim: No end tracking of dynein was observed when the motor complex was mixed with only EB1, BICD2N and LIS1.
source: No end tracking of dynein was observed when the motor complex was mixed with only EB1, BICD2N and LIS1 (32 growth phases analysed), confirming the essential role of dynactin in inducing this behaviour.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data (32 growth phases analyzed with no tracking observed).

claim: LIS1 can promote EB1- and dynactin-dependent tracking of dynein on growing plus ends in the presence and absence of BICD2N in the assay chamber.
source: Thus, LIS1 can promote EB1- and dynactin-dependent tracking of dynein on growing plus ends in the presence and absence of BICD2N in the assay chamber.
evidence: This claim represents a conclusion drawn from the experimental data in Figures 2 and 4.

claim: The inclusion of both CLIP-170 and LIS1 did not alter the site of transport initiation of dynein-dynactin-BICD2N complexes in the presence of EB1.
source: The inclusion of both CLIP-170 and LIS1 did not alter the site of transport initiation of dynein-dynactin-BICD2N complexes in the presence of EB1 (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2A.

claim: CLIP-170 did not affect the frequency or duration of plus-end tracking events of dynein observed in the presence of EB1, dynactin, BICD2N and LIS1.
source: Furthermore, CLIP-170 did not affect the frequency or duration of plus-end tracking events of dynein observed in the presence of EB1, dynactin, BICD2N and LIS1 (Figure 4—figure supplement 2B–E).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2B–E.

claim: EB1, but not LIS1 or CLIP-170, is a key factor in targeting processive dynein-dynactin-BICD2N complexes to the plus ends of growing microtubules in the assay system.
source: We conclude that EB1, but not LIS1 or CLIP-170, is a key factor in targeting processive dynein-dynactin-BICD2N complexes to the plus ends of growing microtubules in our assay system.
evidence: This claim represents a conclusion drawn from the experimental data in Figure 4 and Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: In the presence of EB1, dynactin, BICD2N and LIS1, only 10% of minus end-directed movements from the plus end initiated from a plus-end tracking event of dynein.
source: Indeed, further analysis revealed that in the presence of EB1, dynactin, BICD2N and LIS1, only 10% of minus end-directed movements from the plus end initiated from a plus-end tracking event of dynein (Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Minus end-directed movements from the plus end almost always occurred immediately after engagement of the motor complex with this site.
source: Instead, minus end-directed movements from the plus end almost always occurred immediately after engagement of the motor complex with this site (Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Dynein complexes that track the plus ends of microtubules rarely act directly as a source of motors for minus end-directed transport in the assay conditions.
source: Thus, dynein complexes that track the plus ends of microtubules rarely act directly as a source of motors for minus end-directed transport in our assay conditions.
evidence: This claim represents a conclusion drawn from the experimental data in Figure 4C.

claim: Alexa647-BICD2N was detected on almost all minus end-directed TMR-dynein complexes.
source: As expected, Alexa647-BICD2N was detected on almost all minus end-directed TMR-dynein complexes (Figure 4—figure supplement 3A), including those that initiated movement immediately after engaging with the growing plus end (Figure 4D, Figure 4—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by co-localization data shown in Figure 4D and Figure 4—figure supplement 3.

claim: Alexa647-BICD2N was detected on ~40% of events in which TMR-dynein tracked the growing plus ends of microtubules.
source: Alexa647-BICD2N was also detected on ~40% of events in which TMR-dynein tracked the growing plus ends of microtubules (Figure 4D,E).
evidence: This claim is supported by co-localization data shown in Figure 4D,E.

claim: The dual-labelled complexes that tracked the plus end never gave rise to minus end-directed transport events.
source: The dual-labelled complexes that tracked the plus end never gave rise to minus end-directed transport events; all 38 dual-labelled complexes that initiated minus end-directed transport from the plus end did so immediately after docking at this site.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data (38 complexes analyzed).

claim: The end tracking complexes containing Alexa647-BICD2N and TMR-dynein are dynein-dynactin-BICD2N complexes that are not capable of minus end-directed movement.
source: Because dynein cannot track growing plus ends without dynactin, we conclude that the end tracking complexes containing Alexa647-BICD2N and TMR-dynein are dynein-dynactin-BICD2N complexes that are not capable of minus end-directed movement.
evidence: This claim represents a conclusion drawn from the experimental data in Figure 4 and the requirement for dynactin in tracking.

claim: LIS1 increased the proportion of microtubule-associated dynein complexes that underwent minus end-directed motion from 45% to 70% in the presence of dynactin and BICD2N.
source: Interestingly, LIS1 increased the proportion of microtubule-associated dynein complexes that underwent minus end-directed motion from 45% to 70% (Figure 5A).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: When the relative concentration of BICD2N was reduced 10-fold, hardly any dynein complexes exhibited minus end-directed transport in the absence of LIS1.
source: When the relative concentration of BICD2N was reduced 10-fold, we observed hardly any dynein complexes exhibiting minus end-directed transport in the absence of LIS1 (Figure 5B,C).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 5B,C.

claim: In the presence of LIS1 and reduced BICD2N concentration, a sizeable fraction of dynein complexes were transported towards the microtubule minus end.
source: In the presence of LIS1, however, a sizeable fraction of dynein complexes were transported towards the microtubule minus end (Figure 5B,C).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 5B,C.

claim: LIS1 can induce dynein transport with dynactin and BICD2N concentrations that are otherwise insufficient to elicit this behaviour.
source: Thus, LIS1 can induce dynein transport with dynactin and BICD2N concentrations that are otherwise insufficient to elicit this behaviour.
evidence: This claim represents a conclusion drawn from the experimental data in Figure 5B,C.

claim: Although LIS1 is not essential for minus end-directed movements of dynein when incubated with dynactin and BICD2N, it can strongly stimulate the frequency of these events.
source: We conclude that although LIS1 is not essential for minus end-directed movements of dynein when incubated with dynactin and BICD2N, it can strongly stimulate the frequency of these events.
evidence: This claim represents a conclusion drawn from the experimental data in Figure 5.

claim: LIS1 strongly increased the association of Alexa647-BICD2N with TMR-dynein in the presence of dynactin.
source: Quantification of fluorescent signals on microtubules revealed that LIS1 strongly increased the association of Alexa647-BICD2N with TMR-dynein in the presence of dynactin (Figure 5B,D).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 5B,D.

claim: LIS1 promotes the assembly of the dynein-dynactin-BICD2N complex.
source: Coupled to previous reports that dynactin is required for association of BICD2N with dynein (Hoang et al., 2017; McKenney et al., 2014; Schlager et al., 2014; Splinter et al., 2012), these data indicate that LIS1 promotes the assembly of the dynein-dynactin-BICD2N complex.
evidence: This claim represents a conclusion drawn from the experimental data in Figure 5 and previous literature.

claim: In the presence of LIS1, the mean and maximum velocity of minus end-directed dynein-dynactin-BICD2N complexes on dynamic microtubules increased markedly.
source: In the presence of LIS1, the mean and maximum velocity of minus end-directed dynein-dynactin-BICD2N complexes on dynamic microtubules also increased markedly, regardless of whether EB1 was included in the assay (Figure 6A,B, Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 6A,B and Figure 6—figure supplement 1.

claim: LIS1 did not strongly affect the run length of motile dynein-dynactin-BICD2N complexes.
source: LIS1 did not, however, strongly affect the run length of motile dynein-dynactin-BICD2N complexes (Figure 6C).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Increased velocity of dynein-dynactin-BICD2N movement was observed over a large range of LIS1 protein concentrations.
source: Increased velocity of dynein-dynactin-BICD2N movement was observed over a large range of LIS1 protein concentrations (Figure 6D).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: There was no significant difference in the mean fluorescent intensity of dynein within minus end-directed transport complexes in the presence and absence of LIS1.
source: There was no significant difference in the mean fluorescent intensity of dynein within minus end-directed transport complexes in the presence and absence of LIS1 (Figure 6E).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 6E.

claim: There was no correlation between the fluorescence intensity of transported dynein complexes and their velocity.
source: Moreover, there was no correlation between the fluorescence intensity of transported dynein complexes and their velocity (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: Multimerisation of the motor does not account for LIS1's ability to stimulate dynein velocity.
source: These experiments suggest that multimerisation of the motor does not account for LIS1's ability to stimulate dynein velocity.
evidence: This claim represents a conclusion drawn from the experimental data in Figure 6E and Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: LIS1 strongly inhibits microtubule gliding by purified yeast, porcine or bovine dynein complexes that are immobilised on a glass surface.
source: For instance, LIS1 strongly inhibits microtubule gliding by purified yeast (Huang et al., 2012), porcine (Torisawa et al., 2011; Yamada et al., 2008) or bovine (Wang et al., 2013) dynein complexes that are immobilised on a glass surface.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Human recombinant dyneins adsorbed on a glass surface induced robust gliding of microtubules in the presence of ATP.
source: As documented previously (Hoang et al., 2017; Schlager et al., 2014; Trokter et al., 2012), human recombinant dyneins adsorbed on a glass surface induced robust gliding of microtubules in the presence of ATP (Figure 6F, Figure 6—figure supplement 3A, Video 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6F, Figure 6—figure supplement 3A, and Video 1, as well as citations to previous studies.

claim: Addition of LIS1 to dynein during the surface adsorption step resulted in a dose-dependent inhibition of microtubule translocation.
source: Addition of LIS1 to dynein during the surface adsorption step did not inhibit the subsequent association of microtubules with the glass surface but did result in a dose-dependent inhibition of microtubule translocation (Figure 6F, Figure 6—figure supplement 3A, Video 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6F, Figure 6—figure supplement 3A, and Video 1.

claim: LIS1 could strongly inhibit microtubule gliding without reducing the amount of fluorescently labelled dynein on the glass surface.
source: Confirming this notion, LIS1 could strongly inhibited microtubule gliding without reducing the amount of fluorescently labelled dynein on the glass surface (Figure 6—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 3B.

claim: Microtubules did not stably associate with glass surfaces incubated with only LIS1.
source: We also confirmed that microtubules did not stably associate with glass surfaces incubated with only LIS1 (Video 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Video 2.

claim: LIS1 does not directly interact with microtubules.
source: This finding corroborates the results of previous studies showing that LIS1 does not directly interact with microtubules (McKenney et al., 2010; Yamada et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data in Video 2 and citations to previous studies.

claim: LIS1 can directly inhibit the ability of human recombinant dynein to glide microtubules.
source: We conclude that LIS1 can directly inhibit the ability of human recombinant dynein to glide microtubules.
evidence: This claim represents a conclusion drawn from the experimental data in Figure 6 and Figure 6—figure supplement 3.

claim: LIS1 exerts different functional effects on ensembles of isolated human dynein complexes in a gliding assay and on individual dynein-dynactin-BICD2N complexes running along immobilised microtubules.
source: Thus, LIS1 exerts different functional effects on ensembles of isolated human dynein complexes in a gliding assay and on individual dynein-dynactin-BICD2N complexes running along immobilised microtubules.
evidence: This claim represents a conclusion drawn from comparing the experimental data in Figure 6 with the gliding assay results.

claim: TMR-LIS1 was co-transported with the vast majority of processive Alexa647-labelled dynein-dynactin-BICD2N complexes.
source: In addition to frequently associating with Alexa647-dynein complexes that tracked the growing plus end or exhibited non-processive behaviour on the lattice (Figure 7—figure supplement 1), TMR-LIS1 was co-transported with the vast majority of processive Alexa647-labelled dynein-dynactin-BICD2N complexes (Figure 7A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by co-localization data shown in Figure 7A,B.

claim: The mean velocity of minus end-directed dynein complexes with a TMR-LIS1 signal was similar to that observed in previous experiments using unlabelled LIS1.
source: The mean velocity of minus end-directed dynein complexes with a TMR-LIS1 signal (Figure 7C) was similar to that observed in the previous experiments using unlabelled LIS1 (Figure 6B).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison of quantitative data shown in Figure 7C and Figure 6B.

claim: The subset of minus end-directed Alexa647-dynein complexes that did not have a TMR-LIS1 signal moved with a significantly reduced speed compared to those that did.
source: Within the same imaging chambers, the subset of minus end-directed Alexa647-dynein complexes that did not have a TMR-LIS1 signal moved with a significantly reduced speed compared to those that did (Figure 7C).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: LIS1 regulates the velocity of dynein-dynactin-BICD2N transport complexes by associating with them.
source: These data indicate that LIS1 regulates the velocity of dynein-dynactin-BICD2N transport complexes by associating with them.
evidence: This claim represents a conclusion drawn from the experimental data in Figure 7.

claim: Many dyneins that tracked the plus end during a growth phase did not dissociate from this site when a shrinkage event began and instead retreated with the depolymerising end.
source: Many dyneins that tracked the plus end during a growth phase did not dissociate from this site when a shrinkage event began and instead retreated with the depolymerising end (Figure 8A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8A,B.

claim: Dynein bound to a lattice site could retreat with the shrinking end when the depolymerisation process swept through its binding site, including in the absence of EB1.
source: Dynein bound to a lattice site could also retreat with the shrinking end when the depolymerisation process swept through its binding site, including in the absence of EB1 (Figure 8A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8A.

claim: The association of dynein with shrinking microtubule ends could last for several seconds, during which time hundreds of tubulin subunits dissociate from the plus end.
source: The association of dynein with shrinking microtubule ends could last for several seconds, during which time hundreds of tubulin subunits dissociate from the plus end (Karr et al., 1980).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data and citation to a study on tubulin dissociation rates.

claim: EB1 is not needed for association of dynein with the plus end of shrinking microtubules.
source: Our finding that EB1 is not needed for association of dynein with the plus end of shrinking microtubules is consistent with the observation that EB family members only track plus ends during growth phases (Bieling et al., 2008, 2007; Maurer et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 8 and citations to previous studies on EB protein behavior.

claim: EB proteins do not track shrinking ends in the assay conditions.
source: We confirmed that EB proteins do not track shrinking ends in our assay conditions, including those bound to dynein (Figure 8C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8C.

claim: Although an EB protein is required for dynein to track the plus end during growth, this is not the case during shrinkage.
source: These data indicate that although an EB protein is required for dynein to track the plus end during growth, this is not the case during shrinkage.
evidence: This claim represents a conclusion drawn from the experimental data in Figure 8.

claim: Dynactin appears to be required for the association of dynein with dynamic plus ends during bouts of shrinkage as well as growth.
source: Interestingly, we never observed dynein tracking on a shrinking microtubule plus end in the absence of dynactin (0/103 retention events following encounters of dynein with a shrinking end in the absence of dynactin (Figure 8—figure supplement 1B) vs 123/228 events in the presence of dynactin (Figure 8B)). Thus, dynactin appears to be required for the association of dynein with dynamic plus ends during bouts of shrinkage as well as growth.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 8B and Figure 8—figure supplement 1B.

claim: TMR-LIS1 was detected with Alexa647-dynein in 20 of 22 events in which the motor remained associated with the plus end during shrinkage.
source: TMR-LIS1 was detected with Alexa647-dynein in 20 of 22 events analysed in which the motor remained associated with the plus end during shrinkage (Figure 8—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by co-localization data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1C.

claim: LIS1 significantly increased the frequency of dynein remaining associated with the plus end after encountering a shrinking end in combination with dynactin, EB1 and dynactin, and EB1, dynactin and BICD2N.
source: Further analysis revealed that, although LIS1 was not essential for maintenance of dynein on the plus end after encountering a shrinking end, it did significantly increase the frequency of this behaviour in combination with (i) dynactin, (ii) EB1 and dynactin and (iii) EB1, dynactin and BICD2N (Figure 8B).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 8B.

claim: No altered frequency of shrinking end tracking events of dynein was observed when LIS1 was added to a combination of dynactin and BICD2N.
source: We did not, however, observe an altered frequency of shrinking end tracking events of dynein when LIS1 was added to a combination of dynactin and BICD2N (Figure 8B).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data shown in Figure 8B.

claim: Vanadate strongly inhibited the minus end-directed transport of dynein-dynactin-BICD2N complexes.
source: Vanadate strongly inhibited the minus end-directed transport of dynein-dynactin-BICD2N complexes (Figure 8—figure supplement 1D), providing an internal control for its inhibitory effect on ATP hydrolysis.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Association of dynein with the plus ends of shrinking microtubules was frequently observed in the presence of vanadate.
source: In contrast, association of dynein with the plus ends of shrinking microtubules was frequently observed in the presence of vanadate (Figure 8D), with no statistically significant difference in the occurrence of these events compared to in the presence of only ATP (Figure 8B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8D and quantitative comparison with Figure 8B.

claim: Vanadate did not disrupt end tracking of the full dynein complex during growth phases.
source: We also noted that vanadate did not disrupt end tracking of the full dynein complex during growth phases (Figure 8D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 8D.

claim: The association of dynein with microtubule plus ends during both growth and shrinkage is not dependent on the ATP hydrolysis cycle.
source: Thus, the association of dynein with microtubule plus ends during both growth and shrinkage is not dependent on the ATP hydrolysis cycle.
evidence: This claim represents a conclusion drawn from the experimental data in Figure 8D.

claim: Persistent association of dyneins with dynamic microtubule plus ends could be an intrinsic property of the EB1/dynactin/dynein system.
source: Our data suggest that persistent association of dyneins with dynamic microtubule plus ends could be an intrinsic property of the EB1/dynactin/dynein system.
evidence: This claim represents speculation based on the experimental data and comparison with fungal systems.

claim: The formation of the dynein-dynactin complex is possible at EB1-bound microtubule plus ends in the absence of a cargo adaptor.
source: Our data suggest that the formation of the dynein-dynactin complex is possible at EB1-bound microtubule plus ends in the absence of a cargo adaptor.
evidence: This claim represents an inference drawn from the experimental data showing tracking in the absence of BICD2N.

claim: LIS1's ability to promote the assembly of the dynein-dynactin-BICD2N complex in vitro is consistent with a role in stimulating the association of dynein with dynactin.
source: Our finding that LIS1 can promote the assembly of the dynein-dynactin-BICD2N complex in vitro is consistent with a role in stimulating the association of dynein with dynactin.
evidence: This claim represents an inference drawn from the experimental data in Figure 5.

claim: The ability of EB proteins to bias the initiation of processive transport to the plus ends of microtubules could play a particularly important role in axons.
source: The ability of EB proteins to bias the initiation of processive transport to the plus ends of microtubules could play a particularly important role in axons, where is has been proposed that the initiation of motility in distal regions is a rate-limiting step in retrograde transport processes (Moughamian and Holzbaur, 2012; Moughamian et al., 2013).
evidence: This claim represents speculation based on the experimental data and citations to previous studies.

claim: Factors not included in the in vitro experiments may be able to promote the conversion of plus-end tracking events to minus end-directed transport events in vivo.
source: Factors not included in our in vitro experiments may be able to promote the conversion of plus-end tracking events to minus end-directed transport events in vivo.
evidence: This claim represents speculation about potential in vivo mechanisms.

claim: The changes in speed induced by LIS1 are sizeable, with mean velocity increases in the range of 60–175% depending on the experimental conditions.
source: The changes in speed induced by LIS1 are sizeable, with mean velocity increases in the range of 60–175% depending on the experimental conditions.
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative data from Figure 6.

claim: LIS1 may contribute to the high velocities exhibited by dynein-associated cargoes in vivo.
source: LIS1 may therefore contribute to the high velocities exhibited by dynein-associated cargoes in vivo, which often exceed those of minimal motor complexes in vitro.
evidence: This claim represents speculation based on the experimental data and comparison with in vivo observations.

claim: By prolonging the interaction with dynamic microtubules, an ability of mammalian dynein-dynactin complexes to track shrinking ends would be expected to increase the delivery of the motor complex to other cellular sites.
source: By prolonging the interaction with dynamic microtubules, an ability of mammalian dynein-dynactin complexes to track shrinking ends would be expected to increase the delivery of the motor complex to other cellular sites.
evidence: This claim represents speculation about the functional significance of tracking shrinking ends.
